title: Agentic Postgres capability manifest
description: The only agent-visible capability surface. Empty by default. This file is also the sole authority for the approved scope vocabulary (implementation plan decision C); the code carries no second copy.

schema_version.description: 1, 2 or 3. **A field is FORBIDDEN below the version that introduces it and REQUIRED at or above it** (ADR 0177), and both halves are deliberate: forbidding it earlier keeps a manifest from carrying a field nothing reads at that version, and requiring it keeps the introducing version from being one in which it is optional and therefore absent. v2 adds `version`, `lifecycle` and `risk` for every kind. v3 adds `max_response_bytes` and `max_concurrent_calls` to reads and writes, and `supports_dry_run` and `requires_approval` to writes -- all four FORBIDDEN on a metadata capability, which bounds none of them (ADR 0179). Every older version still loads, because `capabilities.yaml` is a gitignored operator input that exists only on the host: a schema refusing one outright would fail the next deploy on a file no commit can fix.

capabilities.description: Enabled agent tools. An entry may exist while disabled; enabling one requires a live backing API contract.

allOf.description: The v2 gate, at the document level rather than per capability, because a manifest declaring one version and mixing two shapes is the state this exists to refuse (ADR 0177). `minimum: 2` rather than `const: 2` since v3 arrived: a field introduced at v2 stays required at every version above it, and `const` would have made v3 a version in which the three were forbidden again.

The v3 gate (ADR 0179). Required by KIND rather than uniformly: a read and a write both produce a response and both take a concurrency slot, and only a write has anything to not-do, so only a write declares a dry run and an approval. A metadata capability is forbidden all four by `$defs/capability`'s own branch -- stated there rather than here, because it is a fact about the kind and not about the version.

scope.description: Every approved scope name: the union of three closed classes, and the classes are the point (ADR 0079, ADR 0100). DATA scopes are one per (frozen-domain resource, verb) plus meta:read for schema introspection, closed by docs/decisions/0003-example-domain.md and growing only when that is superseded. STORAGE scopes are one per (object, verb) over the object-storage surface, closed by that surface. ADMINISTRATIVE scopes are one per (platform identity resource, verb) over the auth service's own surface, closed by that surface. All three classes are LISTED; the administrative one was derived as this union less the other two until ADR 0100, and that sentence outlived the change by two sessions -- see $defs/administrative_scope, which has said so since Session 7 Run 1. A name added here and to no class raises where the registry is read: see scope_registry.assert_classes_partition_the_vocabulary. A capability manifest may request only the data class: see $defs/agent_scope.

agent_scope.description: The scopes a capability manifest may declare in required_scopes: the data class only. An administrative scope is issuable to a human administrator's token and is not requestable by a tool manifest. ADR 0006 rejected a pattern-validated vocabulary precisely because it would accept admin:everything, and one enum serving both purposes reintroduces that by another route. A STORAGE scope is absent for the same reason and one more: object storage is human-only in Session 7, and this $ref is where that is enforced rather than asserted.

storage_scope.description: The object-storage class (ADR 0100). One per (object, verb) over the storage surface, closed by that surface. Referenced by no other schema member on purpose: it exists so the partition can be checked.

administrative_scope.description: The platform identity class (ADR 0079), one per (platform identity resource, verb) over the auth service's own surface, closed by that surface. LISTED here since ADR 0100; it used to be derived as the union less the data class, which is correct for two classes and silently wrong for three -- a name in the union and in no class was absorbed into this one, classified by arithmetic rather than by a decision. Measured in Session 7 Run 1. The three classes are now checked against the union exactly: see scope_registry.assert_classes_partition_the_vocabulary. admin_audit:read joined in Session 9 Run 7 with no :write twin, and the asymmetry is the decision rather than an omission: app_private.agent_audit is append-only, its own COMMENT says so, and the only paths in are the definer functions that write it. A scope naming a write nobody can perform would be a name for an authority that does not exist.

name.description: The capability's stable name, and the MCP tool name unless `tool` says otherwise (ADR 0120). A capability is the AUTHORIZATION unit -- one (resource, verb), which is what required_scopes bounds -- and a tool is a name an agent calls. Those were the same thing until Session 8, when query_resource needed two resources behind one name. Unique across the manifest, enforced by config.load_capabilities_manifest.

tool.description: The MCP tool this capability is exposed through. Absent means the tool is this capability's own `name`, which is every case but one. Present, it groups capabilities: `query_notes` and `query_tasks` both declare `query_resource`, so one tool carries two frozen resources with a SEPARATE scope requirement each (ADR 0120). That is what the capability plan's "notes:read or tasks:read" means, and it is unrepresentable in a single entry -- required_scopes is a conjunction, so one entry naming both would refuse an agent holding either. Capabilities sharing a tool must agree on `kind` and `operation.source`; the compiler refuses them otherwise, because one name with two authorization models is two tools wearing one label.

version.description: The capability's own semantic version, required at schema_version 2 (ADR 0177). Read by the compiler, which carries it into the canonical contract and the deployed lock, and published in docs/mcp-tool-catalog.md. It reaches app_private.agent_audit in Session 16 Run 3, which is where AGT-CAPVER-001 is proved -- this run gives the field a reader, not the whole requirement. No leading zeroes and no pre-release suffix: the pattern is deliberately narrower than semver.org's, because a range nobody compares over is a string, and the comparison this repository needs is equality against what a lock recorded.

lifecycle.description: Where the capability is in its life, required at schema_version 2 (ADR 0177). **`retired` may not be `enabled: true`, and the compiler refuses it** -- which is not a new rule but the existing one reached by a declaration: `compile_canonical` already drops disabled capabilities entirely, because "a runtime that received them would have to be trusted to ignore them, and the lock is meant to be the thing that cannot be argued with". So retirement is enforced by the lock's ABSENCE rather than by a runtime check somebody could forget. `deprecated` compiles in and stays callable, and travels into the lock and the catalog so an operator can see what is on its way out; a lifecycle that refused a deprecated call would make the word mean `retired` and leave one of the two states unreachable. No default, because a default is a value nobody chose.

risk.description: What is at stake when this capability runs, required at schema_version 2 (ADR 0177). **Validated in this run, not yet behavioural**: a metadata capability must be `low` -- it reaches no backend, holds no credential and answers from the lock, so any other value would describe a hazard that does not exist -- and a write may not be `low`, because it changes rows. AGT-RISK-001 requires risk to SELECT a behaviour, and that lands in Run 3 with the denial taxonomy and the audit columns. It deliberately does not narrow a budget: rows, bytes, elapsed time and concurrency are independent by decision (ADR 0129), and a risk class tightening one of them would be a second authority over it.

kind.description: `read` reaches a backend and returns rows; `write` reaches one and changes rows; `metadata` reaches NOTHING and answers from the deployed capability lock (ADR 0120). The third member exists because `list_resources` and `describe_resource` would otherwise have to declare a resource, columns and max_rows describing a query they never make -- values invented to satisfy a schema, which the next reader cannot tell from the real ones (D267). A metadata capability is FORBIDDEN those fields by the allOf below, so "this tool cannot reach a backend" is a property of the manifest rather than of the runtime's good behaviour.

enabled.description: Enabling requires the referenced live OpenAPI operation to exist with a matching approved shape.

operation.description: Reference to one pre-existing operation. Never SQL, never a raw query string, never a runtime-selected name.

source.description: Where the backing operation lives. `lock` is the deployed capability lock itself and is the only source a `metadata` capability may name -- it is not a service, holds no credential and answers no query.

operation_id.description: One operation, named by a DERIVED identifier (ADR 0119): `<object>.<method>`, with `/` written as `.` because the pattern permits neither `/` nor `:`. So `notes.get` and `rpc.create_note.post`. Derived rather than copied, because the live PostgREST publishes no operationId at all -- measured on the locked image: Swagger 2.0, every operation without one. capability_compiler.derive_operation_id is the single authority for the spelling, and the compiler resolves every id against the REVIEWED SURFACE CONTRACT rather than against the served document: the contract is hand-written and can disagree with the catalog (ADR 0050), while the document is an observation. Never a path, never a query string, never a name chosen at request time.

resource.description: Approved API resource, for read capabilities.

columns.description: Frozen column allowlist. Never derived at request time.

max_rows.description: Hard global ceiling a project manifest cannot exceed.

max_response_bytes.description: This capability's own ceiling on one serialized response, narrowing `MAX_SERIALIZED_BYTES` (ADR 0179). **The maximum IS that constant**, so a manifest cannot widen the global bound -- and the number lives in two files, which a contract test keeps equal, because JSON Schema cannot import a Python constant and the choice is between two authorities that are checked and one that is trusted (ADR 0002). Measured, so the value is read against something: a metadata response is 288-683 bytes, a write's is 8-12 KB at 4 KiB of content, and `query_resource` over `notes` reaches the 1 MiB ceiling at 42 rows when each column holds 4 KiB -- against a `max_rows` of 200. The row budget and the byte budget genuinely cross over, at roughly 860 bytes per column, which is ADR 0129's independence claim in numbers. The floor of 1024 is a floor on USEFULNESS: a smaller ceiling could not carry one row of anything.

max_concurrent_calls.description: This capability's own ceiling on simultaneous in-flight calls, narrowing the process-wide semaphore (ADR 0179). **The effective bound is `min(this, process-wide)`, taken at the acquisition** -- and this `maximum` is a sanity cap rather than the real ceiling, because the process-wide bound is rendered from `api.rest.pool_size` at half (ADR 0129) and a capability manifest never sees it. The asymmetry with `max_response_bytes`, whose maximum IS its global, is stated because a reader seeing two maxima would reasonably assume both are the enforcement. Narrowing only: a capability that could raise its own share would be deciding how much of a human-facing pool an agent may take, which is ADR 0070's rule inverted.

supports_dry_run.description: Whether this write can be asked to run its authorization, scope and validation and then stop (ADR 0179). **Declared at v3 and BEHAVING in Session 16 Run 7** (D892): ADR 0177 requires a field at the version that introduces it, and declaring this in a second bump would move the manifest format three times in one session. Writes only -- a read and a metadata call change nothing, so there is nothing for them to not-do.

requires_approval.description: Whether this write is refused pending an approval this product does not implement (D870, ADR 0179). **A declaration and a named refusal, never a workflow**: approval implies a pending request, durable state holding it, a second principal, and a path by which the caller learns the outcome -- the last of which is a notification plane this product does not have. Declared at v3 and refusing in Run 7.

redact.description: Parameters replaced before the audit record is written.

allOf.description: A metadata capability answers from the deployed lock and reaches no backend, so every field describing one is FORBIDDEN rather than merely unrequired (ADR 0120). Stated as a refusal because the alternative is a manifest carrying a resource and a column list for a query nobody makes, which reads exactly like a real backing and is the shape D267 refuses in a comment.

A metadata capability reaches no backend, holds no credential and answers from the deployed lock, so `moderate` or `high` would name a hazard that does not exist (ADR 0177). Written as a constraint on the value rather than as a required field, so it says nothing at schema_version 1, where `risk` is absent.

A write changes rows, so `low` is a claim the kind contradicts (ADR 0177). The pair with the branch above is the whole of what `risk` reads in Session 16 Run 2; the behaviour AGT-RISK-001 asks for arrives in Run 3.
